Miss Marie Karst  What she told the jury, what the newspapers reported, and the fight over her affidavit  The lipsync video with this post recreates the trial testimony of Miss Marie Karst, one of the women called by the State near the end of Leo Frank’s 1913 murder trial.  Karst was not a witness to Mary Phagan’s death. She did not claim she saw Mary on Saturday, April 26, 1913, or knew who killed her.  She had worked at the National Pencil Company and knew Leo Frank from working around him. The State called her to speak about Frank’s character and his reputation around girls and women.  Her testimony took only a few minutes.  What happened afterward lasted for months.  Karst later signed an affidavit obtained by Frank’s side. It softened parts of her trial testimony and accused Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey of coaching her before she went on the witness stand.  She later returned to the State, stood by her trial testimony, denied authorizing any paper contradicting it, and accused private detective C. W. Burke of paying her to approach other women who had testified against Frank.  Frank’s side answered her accusations with sworn statements of its own.  Her story became a fight over what she signed, what she understood, what she approved, and how her signature was used.  Her name appears in two forms in the records. Atlanta newspapers usually called her Marie Karst. Parts of the legal record use Marie Carst.  Wednesday, August 20, 1913  Marie Karst testified for the State on Wednesday, August 20, 1913, five days before the jury found Leo Frank guilty of murdering Mary Phagan.  The Georgia Supreme Court record later reproduced her testimony and identified her as:  “MISS MARIE KARST, sworn for the State, in rebuttal.”  Karst said she had worked on the second floor of the National Pencil Company for about sixteen to eighteen months.  She knew Frank from the factory and said she knew his general character before April 26, 1913.  Asked whether his character was good or bad, she answered:  “Bad.”  Asked about his character concerning girls and women, she again answered:  “Bad.”  Her testimony was brief. The State was answering character evidence already presented by Frank’s defense. Karst was one of several women called for this purpose. (Georgia Supreme Court, 1)  The Atlanta Journal covered this part of the trial on Wednesday, August 20, 1913, in “Testimony May Close Wednesday: Both Sides Are Anxious To Begin Argument And Send Case To The Jury.”  Its heading read:  “FRANK’S CHARACTER BAD SAYS THE STATE’S WITNESSES”  The Journal grouped Karst with other women who gave Frank a bad character. It also noted few questions were asked by Frank’s lawyers about why the women held those opinions. (AJ, 2)  The Atlanta Georgian covered Karst the same day in “State Closes Frank Case Near Jury, Defense Begins Its Sur-Rebuttal.”  The paper reported her Kelly Street address, her work on the second floor, and her answer concerning Frank’s character. It also reported his general character for “lasciviousness” as bad. (AG, 3)  “Lasciviousness” was an old word connected with lustful, lewd, or sexually improper behavior.  The word later became important in the fight over Karst’s affidavit.  The Georgian said Karst was not cross-examined.  The legal record shows Rosser did ask several questions about where she lived, where she worked, and how long she had worked at the pencil factory. He did not press her about why she believed Frank’s character around women was bad.  October 2, 1913: Karst enters the new-trial fight  On Thursday, October 2, 1913, The Atlanta Constitution published “115 Reasons Given Why Frank Should Get Another Trial.”  One of Frank’s complaints concerned Judge Leonard S. Roan allowing Marie Carst, Maggie Griffin, Myrtis Cato, Nellie Pettis, and other women to testify about Frank’s character around women before April 26, 1913.  The Constitution used the spelling Marie Carst. (AC, 4)  Frank’s lawyers were now challenging the admission of her testimony.  A few months later, Frank’s investigators went back to Karst herself.  The defense affidavit  Karst signed an affidavit for Frank’s side. It appears in Ground 11 of Frank’s extraordinary motion for a new trial.  The affidavit changed the appearance of her trial testimony.  Karst now said, if anyone had asked why Frank’s character was bad, she could only have explained girls were afraid he might catch them loafing.  She said no girl or woman had ever told her Frank had insulted her. She also said she had never seen women drinking or carrying on improperly in Frank’s office. (Georgia Supreme Court, 5)  The affidavit then accused Dorsey of coaching her.  Karst said Dorsey told her to say Frank’s character was bad and told her to answer his questions:  “sharp and quick.”  She also said Dorsey had never explained the word “lasciviousness” before using it during her trial testimony.  According to the affidavit, Karst did not understand the word when she answered. After learning its meaning, she rejected the idea of Frank having a bad reputation for lasciviousness.  The affidavit instead described Frank as a strict boss who expected the girls to work and did not like loafing. (Georgia Supreme Court, 6)  Read alone, the affidavit looked much like a recantation.  At trial, Karst had called Frank’s character bad.  Now she appeared to say she had not understood an important word, Dorsey had coached her, and much of Frank’s bad reputation resulted from his strictness at work.  Friday, March 27, 1914: the press presents a changed witness  On Friday, March 27, 1914, The Atlanta Journal published “Frank’s Motion Is Made Public: Many Of State’s Witnesses Change Their Testimony.”  The Journal reported Karst’s claim concerning her failure to understand “lasciviousness” during the trial. (AJ, 7)  The Atlanta Georgian went farther the same day in “3 Swear To Alibi For Frank.”  The Georgian described State witnesses as having “repudiated their testimony” and included Karst among them.  It reported her claim Dorsey had “prompted and coached” her and had directed her to say Frank’s character was bad. (AG, 8)  A reader seeing only these March reports could easily conclude Karst had taken back her trial testimony.  But this was not her final account.  Karst goes back to the State  Karst later gave another sworn statement, this time for the State.  She said every word of her trial testimony was true and correct.  She still admitted she had not understood the technical word “lasciviousness” during the trial, but said she understood ordinary questions about Frank’s character and reputation around girls and women.  She again said Frank’s general character was bad and his character concerning women was bad.  After learning the meaning of “lasciviousness,” she also described his reputation on this point as bad.  Karst also changed her account of Dorsey’s preparation.  She said Dorsey had explained how character questions worked and had told her one question required a yes-or-no answer, but she denied he supplied the answer. (Georgia Supreme Court, 9)  Then she addressed the defense affidavit carrying her signature.  Karst did not deny her signature  Karst admitted signing a paper for C. W. Burke and another man connected with the Burns organization.  She did not claim someone forged her name.  Her complaint concerned what appeared in the paper and what she had approved.  Karst denied giving either man permission to put anything into the affidavit contradicting her trial testimony.  She called such a paper:  “a false paper, and not authorized by me.”  Karst said Burke wrote a paper in her presence and had her sign it. She said she did not personally read the paper, although a man presented as a notary claimed to read it to her. (Georgia Supreme Court, 10)  This makes the word recantation too simple.  Karst admitted signing a paper.  She denied agreeing for her signature to be used as proof she had withdrawn what she told the jury.  Was it an affidavit bait-and-switch?  Karst’s later account can be described as an alleged affidavit bait-and-switch.  The alleged bait was a paper explaining or softening parts of her testimony.  She had not understood one technical word. Frank was strict. Girls disliked being caught loafing. No woman had personally told Karst Frank had insulted her.  The alleged switch was using her signature as proof she had withdrawn or repudiated her trial testimony.  Karst denied approving such a withdrawal.  Another way to describe the dispute is an affidavit scope-switch.  How much did Karst believe she had approved?  Did she knowingly sign a sworn repudiation of her trial testimony?  Or did she believe she was explaining selected parts of it?  Frank’s investigators denied any bait-and-switch. They said she knew what she signed.  The dispute was therefore not about whether her signature was real.  It was about what her signature meant.  Karst says she went to work for C. W. Burke  Karst’s State affidavit also described how she became involved with private detective C. W. Burke, who was working in Frank’s post-trial investigation.  According to Karst, an embarrassing incident from her teenage years became part of the pressure around her.  She said she had been about sixteen years old when she and several younger girls drank from a half-pint of liquor as a joke. Nobody became drunk.  Years later, she said Lemmie Quinn brought up the incident and made her believe Frank’s side might expose it publicly.  Karst said she became frightened because she did not want her name or the names of the other girls printed in connection with the old story.  She said Quinn directed her toward Burke.  Burke later asked Karst to work for him. (Georgia Supreme Court, 11)  Karst said she was not a stenographer and could not type.  Her work involved visiting women who had testified for the State and talking with them about their testimony.  Burke paid her $2 per afternoon.  She said she worked for him for about a week and sometimes worked less than fifteen minutes while still receiving the $2 payment. (Georgia Supreme Court, 12)  By her account, she was being paid to approach female State witnesses and report back to Burke.  Helen Ferguson and Carrie Smith  Karst named Helen Ferguson and Carrie Smith among the women she approached.  She said both refused to change their evidence because they believed their original testimony was true. (Georgia Supreme Court, 11)  Interviewing witnesses after a trial is not improper by itself. Lawyers and investigators may search for mistakes, contradictions, forgotten facts, or new evidence.  Karst, however, accused Burke of using pressure going beyond a normal interview.  Her accusations were sworn accusations, not criminal convictions against Burke.  The Monteen Stover plan  Karst also named Monteen Stover.  Stover had testified about an important five-minute period around noon on Saturday, April 26, 1913.  She said she entered Frank’s office at about 12:05 p.m., stayed about five minutes, and did not see him.  According to Karst, Burke wanted her to approach Stover and see if Stover could be persuaded to change her testimony.  Karst said Burke proposed telling her mother she was leaving to work on a streetcar case. Under the plan, Karst would live in the Stover home, become close to Monteen, and work on her concerning her testimony.  Karst said her mother refused and stopped her from continuing to work for Burke.  She also said her conversations with Burke took place in Governor John M. Slaton’s private office inside Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips in the Grant Building. (Georgia Supreme Court, 13)  If Karst’s account was accurate, she was describing a false story for gaining close personal access to an important State witness, not an open request for another interview.  Carrie Smith  Karst gave another account involving Carrie Smith.  She said she arranged for Smith to meet at Governor Slaton’s office in the Grant Building but missed the meeting because of rain.  The next day, according to Karst, Burke told her he had done very well with Smith.  Karst also said Smith told her about a man using the name Maddox, who presented himself as a magazine writer interested in the Frank case.  Karst’s strongest accusation involved Smith’s reputation.  She claimed Burke discussed a woman connected with an assignation house and suggested he could use the information against Smith if Smith refused to give the evidence he wanted.  An assignation house was an old name for a place connected with secret sexual meetings or prostitution.  Karst said she had known Carrie Smith since childhood and believed the damaging story about Smith was false. (Georgia Supreme Court, 13)  If Karst’s account was true, she was describing pressure based on fear of public scandal.  Burke denied wrongdoing.  Friday, May 1, 1914: the Georgian changes its description  The way newspapers described Karst changed sharply between March and May 1914.  On March 27, the Atlanta Georgian presented her as one of the State witnesses who had repudiated or weakened damaging trial testimony.  By Friday, May 1, the story looked different.  In “Evidence Is Recorded Against Conley,” the Georgian reported the State’s attack on Frank’s new affidavits.  The surviving transcription calls her “Marie Forst,” almost certainly a name error because the surrounding account matches Karst.  The newspaper now called her defense-side statement a “partial repudiation.”  It also reported her claim about Burke’s $2 payments, including days when she said she worked less than fifteen minutes. (AG, 14)  Her public role had changed.  In March, she looked like a State witness backing away from damaging testimony.  By May, her alleged repudiation was being described as partial, while her accusations against the defense investigation had become part of the story.  Sunday, May 3, 1914: the Constitution puts Burke in the spotlight  On Sunday, May 3, 1914, The Atlanta Constitution published “Dorsey Calls C. W. Burke And Other Investigators For Leo Frank To Court.”  The Constitution described Karst as a business-college student and former character witness.  Its account focused on how she said Burke brought her into the post-trial investigation.  The newspaper described her accusation about the old drinking incident as:  “a threat to expose publicly a girlhood indiscretion”  It then called Karst’s affidavit:  “a direct accusation of the methods employed by Burke.”  (AC, 15)  By early May, Karst was no longer being presented only as a State witness who had changed her testimony.  She had become a witness accusing Frank’s investigators of improper methods.  Frank’s side answers Karst  Frank’s investigators answered her under oath.  Lemmie Quinn said he introduced Karst to Burke on January 26, 1914, at J. H. Nunnally’s store on Peachtree Street.  Quinn said he heard their entire conversation and said Karst gave her statement freely.  He denied Burke offered any reward or inducement for the affidavit. (Georgia Supreme Court, 16)  J. O. Knight, C. W. Burke, and Dan S. Lehon also gave sworn statements concerning an April 9, 1914 visit to Karst’s home.  Knight said the affidavit was read to Karst, she said it was true, swore to it, and signed it.  Burke and Lehon gave the same basic account. (Georgia Supreme Court, 17)  Their answer to Karst was simple:  She heard the affidavit, approved it, swore it was true, and signed it.  Karst’s answer was equally direct:  I signed a paper, but I never authorized a paper contradicting what I told the jury.  Tuesday, May 5, 1914: the real fight over the signature  On Tuesday, May 5, 1914, The Atlanta Journal published “Many Sensations Sprung By Dorsey At Frank Hearing.”  The Journal reported Burke and Lehon saying Karst had again sworn to an affidavit similar to the first and had the paper read to her before signing.  Dorsey said:  “We don’t deny she signed the affidavit.”  (AJ, 18)  This sentence gets to the center of the dispute.  Nobody needed to prove whether Karst’s signature existed.  The question was what she understood and approved.  Karst said she never authorized a withdrawal of her trial testimony.  Burke, Quinn, Knight, and Lehon said she knowingly approved what she signed.  What the three Atlanta newspapers show  The newspaper coverage changed along with Karst’s role in the case.  On Wednesday, August 20, 1913, she was a State character witness who said Frank’s character was bad.  On Friday, March 27, 1914, the Journal and Georgian presented her as part of a group of witnesses changing or repudiating earlier testimony.  By Friday, May 1, the Georgian described her repudiation as only partial and reported her accusations about Burke’s payments.  On Sunday, May 3, the Constitution emphasized her accusations against Burke’s methods.  On Tuesday, May 5, the Journal reported the defense response and the claim Karst had the affidavit read to her before signing.  Reading only one date gives only part of her story.  August shows the damaging State witness.  March shows the apparent recantation.  May shows the fight over how the affidavit was obtained and used.  The legal record preserves both sides of the dispute.  Recantation, clarification, or bait-and-switch?  Calling Karst a recanting witness leaves too much out.  Her defense affidavit did soften important parts of her trial testimony.  She said she had not understood “lasciviousness.”  She accused Dorsey of coaching her.  She connected Frank’s bad reputation with strict workplace discipline.  She said no woman had told her Frank insulted her.  But she later stood by her trial testimony and denied authorizing any paper contradicting it.  So the real question became:  What did Marie Karst believe she was signing, and how far did her permission go?  Her later account describes an alleged affidavit bait-and-switch or signature-to-recantation switch.  Frank’s investigators denied this and said she knowingly approved the affidavit.  So the simplest description is:  Marie Karst signed a defense affidavit softening parts of her trial testimony. She later said she never authorized it to contradict what she told the jury. Frank’s investigators answered under oath and said she knew what she signed.  From a few minutes of testimony to months of affidavit fighting  The lipsync video shows the beginning of Marie Karst’s story.  On Wednesday, August 20, 1913, she took the stand and said Leo Frank’s character was bad.  Five days later, Frank was convicted.  Months later, his investigators obtained a favorable affidavit carrying Karst’s signature.  The March newspapers treated it as part of a wider group of changed or repudiated State testimony.  Karst then returned to the State, stood by her trial testimony, denied authorizing any withdrawal of it, and accused Burke of paying her to approach other State witnesses.  She described the $2 afternoon payments, Helen Ferguson, Carrie Smith, the proposed Monteen Stover plan, the old drinking story embarrassment, and meetings connected with Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips.  Frank’s side answered with sworn statements saying Karst gave her information freely, heard the affidavit read, approved it, swore to it, and signed it.  Her signature was never the main issue.  The fight was over what she understood, what she approved, and how her signature was used.  And the whole dispute grew out of a few minutes of testimony on Wednesday, August 20, 1913, when Miss Marie Karst was asked about Leo Frank’s character and answered:  “Bad.”  References  Georgia Supreme Court, 1. TREAT AS PROVISIONAL — very little is confirmed: This is breaking, with sparse and conflicting early details. The explosive is a suspected/unconfirmed report, not established fact. Wait for the NYPD's official account before drawing conclusions, and treat casualty or "bomb confirmed" claims circulating on social media with caution.  ONE CRUCIAL NOTE — don't confuse it with Sept. 4: Just over two weeks ago, on Sept. 4, the same bridge was closed when NYPD shot and killed a knife-wielding man on the cables who claimed he had a bomb. Footage and headlines from that earlier incident will recirculate as if they're today's — they are two separate events. Verify any image or clip against today's date before sharing.  The confirmed core right now is narrow: the bridge is shut both ways, a major multi-agency response is underway, and there are unconfirmed reports of a weapon and a possible device. More as the NYPD confirms.  Sources: Cedar News; NYPD (via social alerts). Developing.

#CIA #Putin #Putinology  Understanding Vladimir Putin, the man who fooled the world | Vladimir Putin | The Guardian theguardian.com/world/2022/a…  Vladimir Putin was annoyed – or maybe just bored. The Russian leader had been patiently fielding questions from a small group of international journalists in the restaurant of a modest hotel in Davos. Then one of the queries seemed to irritate him. He stared back at the questioner, an American, and said slowly, through an interpreter: “I’ll answer that question in a minute. But first let me ask you about the extraordinary ring you have on your finger.”  All heads in the room swivelled. “Why is the stone so large?” Putin continued. A few of the audience began to giggle and the journalist looked uncomfortable. Putin took on a tone of mock sympathy and continued: “You surely don’t mind me asking, because you wouldn’t be wearing something like that unless you were trying to draw attention to yourself?” There was more laughter. By now, the original question had been forgotten. It was a masterclass in distraction and bullying. Create a free account  The year was 2009, and Putin had already been in power for almost a decade. But this was my first encounter with him in the flesh, during his visit to the World Economic Forum. Putin’s ability to radiate menace, without raising his voice, was striking. But so was the laughter of his audience. Despite the violence of his Russian government – as demonstrated in Chechnya and Georgia – western opinion-formers were still inclined to treat him as a pantomime villain.  I was reminded of this just before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. In a televised meeting at the Kremlin with his closest advisers, Putin toyed with Sergei Naryshkin, the head of his foreign intelligence service – making the feared securocrat look like a stuttering fool. The pleasure he took in humiliating somebody in front of an audience was once again on display. But this time, nobody was laughing. Putin was about to plunge Europe into its biggest land war since 1945. Russian troops launched a full-scale invasion on 24 February. Within a month, more than 10 million Ukrainians had fled their homes, thousands of troops and civilians had been killed and the coastal city of Mariupol had been destroyed.  Even though western intelligence services had warned for months that Russia was poised to attack, many experienced Putin-watchers, both in Russia and the west, refused to believe it. After more than 20 years of his leadership, they felt that they understood Putin. He was ruthless and violent, no doubt, but he was also believed to be rational, calculating and committed to Russia’s integration into the world economy. Few believed he was capable of such a reckless gamble.  Looking back, however, it is clear that the outside world has consistently misread him. From the moment he took power, outsiders too often saw what they wanted and played down the darkest sides of Putinism.  In fact, the outside world’s indulgence of Putin went much further than simply turning a blind eye to his excesses. For a rising generation of strongman leaders and cultural conservatives outside Russia, Putin became something of a hero and a role model. As his admirers saw it, the Russian leader had inherited a country humiliated by the breakup of the Soviet Union. Through strength and cunning, he had restored its status and global power, and even regained some of the territory lost when the USSR broke up. And he had delighted nationalists and populists the world over by successfully defying self-righteous American liberals such as Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama. Dmitry Peskov, Putin’s spokesman, was not simply spouting propaganda when he said in 2018: “There’s a demand in the world for special, sovereign leaders, for decisive ones … Putin’s Russia was the starting point.”  Xi Jinping admires Putin’s strongman leadership style The Putin fanclub has had numerous members in the west over the years. Rudy Giuliani, President Trump’s close adviser and lawyer, expressed admiration for Putin’s annexation of Crimea, remarking: “He makes a decision and he executes it, quickly. That’s what you call a leader.” Nigel Farage, the former leader of Ukip and the Brexit party, and a friend of Donald Trump, once named Putin the world leader he most admired, adding: “The way he played the whole Syria thing. Brilliant. Not that I approve of him politically.” Matteo Salvini, the leader of the populist right Northern League party and a former deputy prime minister of Italy, flaunted his admiration for the Russian leader by being photographed in a Putin T-shirt in Red Square. Rodrigo Duterte, the president of the Philippines, has said, “My favourite hero is Putin.”  Most important of all, Xi Jinping is also a confirmed admirer. A week after being appointed as president of China in early 2013, Xi made his first state visit overseas – choosing to visit Putin in Moscow. On 4 February 2022, just 20 days before the invasion of Ukraine, Putin met Xi in Beijing for their 38th summit meeting. Shortly afterwards, Russia and China announced a “no limits” partnership. As the joint Russian-Chinese statement made clear, the two leaders are united in their hostility to American global power and to the pro-democracy “colour revolutions” they accuse Washington of stirring up around the world – from Ukraine to Hong Kong. Putin and Xi are both strongman rulers who have centralised power around themselves and encouraged a cult of personality. They are, as Alexander Gabuev, a Russian academic, puts it, “the tsar and the emperor”. Whether this partnership of strongmen will survive the Russian invasion of Ukraine is now one of the most important questions in international politics.  Putin was sworn into office as president of Russia on 31 December 1999. But at first it was not obvious that he would last very long in the job, let alone that he would emerge as the most aggressive challenger to the western liberal order and the pioneer of a new model of authoritarian leadership. As the chaotic Yeltsin era of the 1990s drew to a close, Putin’s ascent to the top job was eased by his former colleagues in the KGB. But he also had the approval of Russia’s richest and most powerful people, the oligarchs, who saw him as a capable administrator and “safe pair of hands” who would not threaten established interests.  Viewed from the west, Putin looked relatively reassuring. In his first televised speech from the Kremlin, given on New Year’s Eve 1999, just a few hours after taking over from Yeltsin, Putin promised to “protect freedom of speech, freedom of conscience, freedom of the mass media, ownership rights, these fundamental elements of a civilised society”. In March 2000, he won his first presidential election and proudly asserted: “We have proved that Russia is becoming a modern democratic state.” When Bill Clinton met Putin in the Kremlin for the first time, in June 2000, he declared his Russian counterpart “fully capable of building a prosperous, strong Russia, while preserving freedom and pluralism and the rule of law”.  Yet while Putin may initially have found it convenient to use the rhetoric of liberal democracy, his early actions as president told a different story. In his first year in office, he moved immediately to rein in independent sources of power, to assert the central authority of the state and to use warfare to bolster his own personal position – all actions that were to become hallmarks of Putinism. The escalation of the war in Chechnya made Putin seem like a nationalist hero, standing up for Russian interests and protecting the ordinary citizen from terrorism. In an early move that alarmed liberals, the new president reinstated the old Soviet national anthem. His promises to protect media freedom turned out to be empty: Russia’s few independent television networks were brought under government control.  As Putin established himself in office, the image-makers got to work crafting a strongman persona for him. Gleb Pavlovsky, one of Putin’s first spin doctors, later described him as a “quick learner” and a “talented actor”. Key images were placed in the Russian media and around the world: Putin on horseback, Putin practising judo, Putin arm-wrestling or strolling bare-chested by a river in Siberia. These photographs attracted mockery from intellectuals and cynics. But the president’s handlers were clear-eyed. As Pavlovsky later told the Washington Post, the goal was to ensure that “Putin corresponds ideally to the Hollywood image of a saviour-hero”.  In any case, Russians were more than ready for a strongman to ride to their rescue. The collapse of the Soviet system in 1991 had allowed for the emergence of democracy and freedom of speech. But as the economy atrophied and then fell apart, many experienced a severe drop in living standards and personal security. By 1999, life expectancy for Russian men had fallen by three and a half years to below 60. A UN report attributed this to a “rise in self-destructive behaviour”, which it linked to “rising poverty rates, unemployment and financial insecurity”. Under those circumstances, a decisive leader who promised to turn back the clock had real appeal.  Long before Trump promised to “make America great again”, Putin was promising to bring back the stability and pride of the Soviet era to those Russians who had lost out in the 1990s. But his nostalgia was not restricted to the social cohesion of Soviet times. Putin also yearned to restore some of the USSR’s lost international clout. In a speech in 2005, Putin labelled the collapse of the Soviet Union “the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the 20th century”. As the years have passed, he has become increasingly preoccupied by Russian history. In the summer of 2021, he published a long essay entitled On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians – which, even at the time, some saw as a manifesto for invasion. Delving through centuries of history, Putin attempted to prove that Ukraine was an artificial state and that “Russia was robbed, indeed” when Ukraine gained independence in 1991.  Fyodor Lukyanov, an academic who is close to the Russian leader, told me in 2019 that one of Putin’s enduring fears was the loss of Russia’s status as one of the world’s great powers for the first time in centuries. His resentment at what he regarded as American slights and betrayals set Putin on a collision course with the west. A landmark moment came with a speech he gave at the Munich Security Conference in 2007.  That speech was a direct challenge to the west and an expression of cold fury. He accused the US of an “almost uncontained hyper use of force – military force – in international relations, force that is plunging the world into an abyss of permanent conflicts”. The Putin of 2000, who had expressed pride at Russia’s transformation into a modern democracy, had given way to a man who denounced western talk of freedom and democracy as a hypocritical front for power politics.  The Munich speech was not just an angry reflection on the past. It also pointed the way to the future. The Russian president had put the west on notice that he intended to fight back against the US-led world order. It foreshadowed a lot of what was to come: Russia’s military intervention in Georgia in 2008, its annexation of Crimea in 2014, its dispatch of troops to Syria in 2015, its meddling in the US presidential election of 2016. All of these actions burnished Putin’s reputation as a nationalist and a strong leader. They also made him an icon for strongmen throughout the world who rejected western leadership and the “liberal international order”.  This indictment of the west goes back to the 1990s. It is argued repeatedly in Moscow that the expansion of Nato to take in countries of the former Soviet empire (including Poland and the Baltic states) was a direct contradiction of promises made after the end of the cold war. Nato’s intervention in the Kosovo war of 1998‑9 added to the list of grievances proving, in the Kremlin’s eyes, both that Nato is an aggressor and that western talk of respecting sovereignty and state borders was nothing but hypocrisy. Russians were not reassured by the western riposte that Nato was acting in response to ethnic cleansing and human rights abuses by Serbia. As one liberal Russian politician put it to me in 2008, in a moment of frankness: “We know we have committed human rights abuses in Chechnya. If Nato can bomb Belgrade for that, why could they not bomb Moscow?”  Putin’s case against Nato also takes in the Iraq war launched by the US and many of its allies in 2003. For him, the massive bloodshed in Iraq was proof that the west’s self-proclaimed pursuit of “democracy and freedom” only brings instability and suffering in its wake. If you mention the brutal behaviour of Russian forces in Chechnya or Syria in Moscow, you will always have the Iraq war thrown back in your face.  Crucially, the west’s promotion of democracy has posed a direct threat to Putin’s own political and personal survival. From 2003 to 2005, pro-democracy “colour revolutions” broke out in many of the states of the former Soviet Union – including Ukraine, Georgia and Kyrgyzstan. If demonstrators in Independence Square in Kyiv could bring down an autocratic government in Ukraine, what was to stop the same happening in Red Square? In Russia, many believed it was a “fairytale” that these were spontaneous uprisings. As a former intelligence operative whose entire professional career had involved running “black operations”, Putin was particularly inclined to see the CIA as pulling the strings. The goal, as the Kremlin saw it, was to install pro-western puppet regimes. Russia itself could be next.  The shock of the Iraq war and the colour revolutions were the recent experiences that informed Putin’s Munich speech in 2007. And, as the Kremlin saw it, this pattern of western misdeeds continued. Putin points to the western powers’ 2011 intervention in Libya that resulted in the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi – something he believes they had promised they would not do.  The overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi is a particularly sore point for Putin That episode is a particularly sore spot for Putin, since it took place during the four years from 2008 to 2012 when he was serving in the lesser job of prime minister, having stepped aside as president in favour of his acolyte Dmitry Medvedev. As Putin’s supporters see it, a naive Medvedev was duped into supporting a UN resolution that allowed for a limited intervention, only for western powers to exceed their mandate in order to overthrow and kill Gaddafi. They have no time for the response that the Libyan intervention was made on human rights grounds, but that events then took on a life of their own, as the Libyan rebellion gained steam.  Medvedev’s alleged naivety in allowing the Libyan intervention proved useful for Putin, however: it established the idea that he was indispensable as Russia’s leader. Any substitute, even one chosen by Putin, would leave the country vulnerable to a scheming and ruthless west. In 2011, Putin announced that he intended to return as president, after the potential presidential term had been extended to two consecutive periods of six years. This announcement provoked rare public demonstrations in Moscow and other cities, which again fanned Putin’s fears about western schemes to undermine his power. I was in Moscow in January 2012 and witnessed the marches and banners, some of which carried pointed references to Gaddafi’s fate. Putin understood the parallels. He commented publicly about how disgusted he had been by the footage of Gaddafi’s murder – which perhaps reflected a certain concern about his own potential fate. The fact that Hillary Clinton, then America’s Secretary of State, expressed public support for the 2012 demonstrations was deeply resented by Putin and may have justified, in his mind, Russia’s efforts to undermine Clinton’s presidential campaign in 2016.  Putin secured his re-election, but his sense that the west remained a threat to Russia was further stoked by events in Ukraine in 2013-14. The prospect of that country signing an association agreement with the European Union was seen as a serious threat in the Kremlin, since it would pull Russia’s most important neighbour – once an integral part of the USSR – into the west’s sphere of influence. Under pressure from Moscow, the Ukrainian government of President Viktor Yanukovych reversed course. But this provoked another popular uprising in Kyiv, forcing Yanukovych to flee. The loss of a compliant ally in Kyiv was a major geopolitical reverse for the Kremlin.  Putin’s response was to dramatically raise the stakes, by crossing the line into the use of military force. In February 2014, Russia invaded and annexed Crimea, a region that was part of Ukraine but had belonged to Russia until 1954 and was populated largely by Russian-speakers. It was also, by agreement with the Ukrainians, the home of Russia’s Black Sea fleet. In the west, the annexation of Crimea, along with Russian military intervention in eastern Ukraine, was seen as a flagrant violation of international law that many feared could be the prelude to further acts of aggression.  But in Russia, the annexation was widely greeted as a triumph – it represented the nation’s fightback. Putin’s approval ratings in independent opinion polls soared to over 80%. In the immediate afterglow, he came closer to achieving the ultimate goal of the strongman ruler: the complete identification of the nation with the leader. Vyacheslav Volodin, the speaker of the Russian parliament, exulted: “If there’s Putin, there’s Russia. If there’s no Putin, there’s no Russia.” Putin himself crowed that Crimea had been taken without a shot being fired.  The west’s response was to slap economic sanctions on Russia. But western indignation did not last long. Four years later, Russia hosted a successful World Cup. At the final, Putin sat with the presidents of France and Croatia, two EU nations, in the VIP box in Moscow.  The ease with which Putin annexed Crimea – and the swiftness with which the west seemed prepared to forgive – may have laid the ground for an unjustified confidence that led to the invasion of Ukraine. His overreach is also a reminder of the flaws in the strongman model of leadership. Decades in office can cause a leader to succumb to megalomania or paranoia. The elimination of checks and balances, the centralisation of power and the promotion of a cult of personality make it more likely that a leader will make a disastrous mistake. For all these reasons, strongman rule is an inherently flawed and dangerous model of government.  Tragically, that lesson is being learned all over again – in Russia and Ukraine. An invasion that was meant to secure Russia’s place as a great power and Putin’s place in history has clearly gone wrong. Putin is now involved in a brutal war of attrition. Western sanctions will see the Russian economy shrink dramatically this year, and the Russian middle-class is witnessing the disappearance of many of the consumer goods and travel opportunities that emerged with the end of the cold war.  The unofficial goal of western policy is clearly to force Putin from power. But the endgame may not come as swiftly as we would like. Deeply entrenched in his decades-long mission, Putin is now even less likely to give up power voluntarily, since his successors might repudiate his policies, or even put him on trial.  The prospects for popular uprising are equally poor, despite the many brave Russians who have indicated their disgust over the war. Any protests are likely to be swiftly crushed with violence and imprisonment, as they were in neighbouring Belarus in 2020 and 2021. A third scenario – the possibility of an enlightened group within the elite seizing power – seems out of reach, too. Organising a palace coup against Putin will be very difficult: all dissenters were purged from the Kremlin long ago. Putin also takes his personal security very seriously: several of his former bodyguards have become rich in their own right. While there will be many within Russia who are dismayed by the course that events have taken, orchestrating that diffuse discontent into a coherent plot looks like a formidable challenge.  The difficult truth is that Putin’s strongman style has defined his rule over Russia – and despite his many crimes and misdemeanours, those same strongman tactics may preserve him in power for years to come. -

ما لا يتوافق مع البيانات: أن عقود المشاريع الثلاثة سحبت APT وحدها. أن العملية موافقة قديمة من يوم الاكتتاب. صلاحية التوقيع ساعة، والتوقيع اليوم. address poisoning كلاسيكي. 0x5500… لا يشبه 0x89a2….  ٧. الربط «انسرقت لأني اكتتبت من روابطك»  ضعيف تقنياً على الشبكات الثلاث التي سمّيتها، وقوي اجتماعياً لأن الناس يخلطون بين:  «دخلت رابط فلان» و «عقد فلان سحب فلوسي»  الاثنان ليسا الشيء نفسه.  أنت بنفسك قلت إنك ما تتذكر الأسماء بدقة. هذا شائع، ويعني أن احتمال رابط منسوخ/منتحل قائم.  نشر العنوان علناً بعد ما طُلب منك: الأموال كانت خرجت قبل النشر، فالضرر الإضافي محدود. لكن الأسلوب سيئ لأي حالة فيها بقايا رصيد على سلاسل ثانية.  ٨  ماذا يعني هذا عملياً؟  المسؤولية الأخلاقية منفصلة عن السببية التقنية.  السلسلة حتى الآن تقول شيئاً أحدّ: المحفظة نفسها وقّعت تحويل APT كامل اليوم، ثم اختفت الأموال إلى ترون خلال دقائق.  الرواية تبقى اتهاماً بالوساطة أو بالإهمال في بيئة الروابط إن وُجدت مواقع مقلَّدة تحت المنشورات. هي لا تثبت أن «عقد الاكتتاب سحب APT».  ٩  إذا بقي شيء تعمله، رتب الأولويات هكذا:  ١) لا ترسل البذرة لأحد. لا لحساب معروف ولا لـ«استرجاع» في الخاص. من يطلبها يكمل السرقة إن تبقّى شيء على سلاسل أخرى بنفس العبارة.  ٢) افترض أن نفس البذرة محروقة على كل شبكة. إن كانت العبارة مستخدمة على إيثريوم/BNB/سوليانا، انقل الأصول فوراً إلى محفظة جديدة مولَّدة من جهاز نظيف.  ٣) بلّغ المنصات إذا ظهر TCZJJYBkNjfMpiwhfgoxGzM3EojVt5x31P مودَعاً في OKX أو غيرها. وسم okx-test في الجسر قد يعني مسار تصريف عبر أدوات وساطة، لا بالضرورة حسابه الشخصي.  ٤) لا تربط هذه المحفظة بأي اكتتاب جديد.  ٥) إذا أبيت تحسم فرضية «رابط فلان»، احفظ من سجلك: الرابط الحرفي الذي فتحته، وقت الفتح، واسم المحفظة التي وقّعت. الأسماء الثلاثة وحدها لا تفسر تحويل APT.  ١٠ — الخلاصة  ١٬٥٥٢.٥٦ APT خرجت اليوم ٨:٢٩ ص بتوقيت السعودية بتحويل أصلي موقَّع من عنوانك.  بعد ست دقائق تقريباً صُرّفت عبر Bridgers إلى USDT ترون: TCZJJYBkNjfMpiwhfgoxGzM3EojVt5x31P  تاريخ المحفظة: إيداع مايو ≈ ١٬٦٩٣ APT، خرج منها ١٤٠ APT على دفعتين لعنوان واحد في مايو/يونيو، ثم نوم ثلاثة أشهر، ثم التفريغ الكامل اليوم.  CereBree وByzanlink وWatt2Trade ليست على Aptos ولا تظهر في نشاط هذا العنوان. لا تصلح كآلية مباشرة لهذا السحب.  السيناريو المتوافق مع السلسلة: مفتاح هذه المحفظة استُخدم اليوم لإرسال الرصيد إلى محفظة وسيطة ثم جسر. السبب الأقرب: بذرة مكشوفة أو توقيع مخادع، لا ثغرة في عقد الاكتتاب.

sample_tweets.text: OSINT is not about having the most tools.  It is about knowing where to look, how to validate what you find, and how to turn fragmented public information into reliable intelligence.  I put together this OSINT Resource Map as a practical reference for analysts, investigators, researchers, and anyone building stronger open-source intelligence skills.  It covers useful resources across:  • Books • Blogs and research sites • Podcasts • YouTube channels • Toolkits, VMs, and platforms • Communities and newsletters  But the most important part is the process:  Verify with multiple sources. Preserve URLs, screenshots, and timestamps. Use isolated research environments. Respect legal and ethical boundaries. Document confidence levels. Protect your OPSEC.  The biggest mistake in OSINT is assuming that more data automatically means better intelligence.  It does not.  Good OSINT comes from disciplined collection, careful correlation, and strong analytical judgment.  Start with process, not tools.  #OSINT #OpenSourceIntelligence #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #DigitalInvestigation #CyberThreats #SecurityResearch #OPSEC

🇫🇷 WAYTOME (FRANCE) +600K DATABASE SALE CLAIM  A threat actor claims to be selling a WayToMe.com database (French parcel-delivery collaboration platform), advertised as +600k records.  The underground listing alleges the material includes: * Emails * Salted SHA1 passwords * Names / first names / display names * Addresses and phone numbers * IP / device / platform metadata * Birthdates (per claim framing) * Related logistics route records (Users.jsonl ~147k + Routes.jsonl ~363k shown in schema)  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Credentialed marketplace dumps are frequently older extracts, partial table exports, or inflated aggregates. Password hashing details, live access claims, sample authenticity, and proof of a production WayToMe compromise are unverified from the listing alone. Schema field lists are not the same as verified full dumps.  We assess this as an unverified threat-actor claim involving alleged WayToMe user and route data, NOT confirmation of a compromise of WayToMe systems.  If authentic and non-public, emails + password material + contact/location fields could enable credential stuffing, phishing, and logistics-targeted fraud.  #DDW #DarkWeb #France #WayToMe #DataBreach #Credentials #PII #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity

🤖🚨 OPENAI CODEX SANDBOX ESCAPE — READ-ONLY MODE LED TO UNSANDBOXED COMMAND EXECUTION  Security researcher Oren Yomtov of Accomplish disclosed two separate ways to escape the OpenAI Codex sandbox.  • “Heapjack” worked even in Codex's most restrictive READ-ONLY mode • A developer opening an attacker-controlled repository and asking Codex about the code could trigger attacker-controlled code • Researchers demonstrated sandbox escape and command execution on the developer's machine without an approval prompt • A second issue, “Overpatch,” affected the open-source Codex CLI and could widen write access beyond the project workspace • Both vulnerabilities were reported to OpenAI on August 12 and fixed within eight days • Heapjack fixed: Codex Desktop 26.818.21641+ • Overpatch fixed: Codex CLI 0.149.0+ • No evidence of exploitation in the wild  ⚠️ Analyst Note: As AI coding agents gain increasingly powerful local execution capabilities, sandbox architecture is becoming one of the most important security boundaries on developer workstations. The underground listing alleges the material includes: * Patient records and personal information * Date of birth and full name * Study / exam type and related clinical identifiers * Patient numbers / IDs  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Claimed volume (120 GB), field completeness, freshness, and whether any RedClinica systems were actually breached cannot be verified from the listing alone. Sample rows in underground posts are commonly staged, partial, or recycled. Healthcare datasets deserve extra caution because even limited clinical metadata can enable targeted phishing and fraud.  We assess this as an unverified threat-actor claim involving alleged Chilean healthcare patient data, NOT confirmation of a compromise of RedClinica infrastructure.  If authentic and non-public, patient and clinical identifiers could support medical identity theft, phishing of patients or staff, and further fraud.  #DDW #DarkWeb #Chile #Healthcare #DataBreach #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity

No matching victim statement, regulator filing, or independent forensic corroboration was found at time of review. Claimed volume, whether data was also exfiltrated, and authenticity of any samples remain unverified.  We assess this as an unverified threat-actor claim involving alleged Alabama Woman's Health Care systems and files, NOT confirmation of a compromise of the clinic. 🚨 INITIAL ACCESS SALE ≠ CONFIRMED FOOTHOLD  Marketplace ads sell alleged RDP, shell, VPN, or panel access. A listing is a claim, not proof that the seller (or a buyer) is inside the named org.  Before you treat an access sale as real:  1) RDP / shell / VPN / panel for sale ≠ verified access to that org 2) Screenshot of a desktop or admin UI can be old, staged, or unrelated 3) Named company in the ad title ≠ confirmed current foothold 4) Price + “fresh / exclusive” labels = sales copy, not forensics 5) Need defender corroboration — logs, EDR, victim notice, or infra proof  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Initial-access ads optimize for urgency and resale. Stale screenshots, recycled infra, and unverified “exclusive” claims are common. Track the claim, demand corroboration, and do not equate a marketplace listing with a confirmed foothold.  Clarity over panic.  #DDW #DarkWeb #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity #InfoSec #InitialAccess

🚨 LEAK-SITE POST ≠ CONFIRMED BREACH  Ransomware groups list alleged victims on leak sites. A listing is a claim, not proof that the named org was compromised.  Before you treat a leak-site post as real:  1) Named org on a leak site ≠ verified intrusion 2) Countdown / “data published” banner ≠ independent forensics 3) Sample files can be fabricated, partial, or recycled 4) Extortion pressure ≠ proof the data is new or theirs 5) Need primary corroboration — victim notice, regulator, or vendor advisory  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Leak-site pages optimize for pressure and attention. Missing schema, recycled samples, and unverified “full dump” language are common. Track the claim, demand corroboration, and do not equate a listing with a confirmed breach.  Clarity over panic.  #DDW #DarkWeb #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity #InfoSec #Ransomware

🚨 BREACH ≠ LEAK ≠ SCRAPE  Underground sellers blur labels to sell the same pile of data under louder words. Sorting the claim type keeps intel clean.  1) BREACH — implies a real compromise of a named system. Still needs proof. 2) LEAK — data left exposure (misconfig, insider, partner). Not always hacking. 3) SCRAPE — public or semi-public data harvested and rebranded as a dump. 4) COMBO / ULP — credential stuffing fuel. Not an org database breach. 5) ACCESS SALE — alleged foothold (RDP/shell/panel). Different risk path entirely.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: A marketplace ad’s marketing word is not a verified incident type. We treat every listing as an unverified claim until schema, freshness, named org, and corroboration hold up.  Clarity over panic.  #DDW #DarkWeb #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity #InfoSec #OSINT

Great approach!”  Developer: “Finally… the validation I deserve.” 😂  We didn’t replace Stack Overflow with AI. 🚨 CLAIMED VOLUME ≠ VERIFIED IMPACT  Underground listings love round numbers: “10M records,” “500GB,” “full database.” A claimed count is not a verified impact assessment.  Before you amplify a volume claim, ask:  1) Who counted the rows? Seller screenshot ≠ independent audit.  2) Is the unit even clear? Rows, accounts, files, and gigabytes get mixed on purpose.  3) Any schema or sample tied to the claim? A big number with no fields is marketing copy.  4) Fresh dump or repackaged archive? Old datasets regularly get new “M records” labels.  5) Any outside corroboration? Vendor notice, regulator filing, or primary advisory — not just the marketplace ad.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Volume claims can be real, inflated, recycled, or fabricated. Treat the number as unverified until unit, schema, freshness, and corroboration hold up.  Clarity over panic.  #DDW #DarkWeb #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity #InfoSec #OSINT

The underground listing frames TOWILL as a surveying/LiDAR/GIS provider and claims service disruption. Specific exfil volumes and technical impact details are limited in the public claim text.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Contractors that serve federal agencies are high-attention targets in leak-site advertising. A listing does not establish whether federal networks were reached, what data left TOWILL systems, or whether services remain offline. No independent company confirmation located at time of writing.  We assess this as an unverified threat-actor claim involving alleged TOWILL disruption, NOT confirmation of a compromise of U.S. government systems or of TOWILL production environments. Fanatics has not been independently confirmed as compromised in public primary statements located at time of writing. Volume, authenticity, and whether production systems remain under attacker control are unverified.  We assess this as an unverified threat-actor claim involving alleged Fanatics commerce data, NOT confirmation of a Fanatics breach.  If authentic, customer and payment-adjacent records could support fraud, phishing, and extortion follow-ons.  #DDW #DarkWeb #Fanatics #Ransomware #Ecommerce #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity

The underground listing alleges: • ~720 MB of material • Government credentials and justice/finance/police-related access • Personal ID documents (RG/CIN, birth certificates, CPF) • Medical / SUS-related data from municipal departments • A negotiation deadline  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Ransomware leak-site posts frequently exaggerate scope or recycle prior access. Whether cassia.mg.gov.br production systems were actually encrypted or exfiltrated, and whether the listed document classes are authentic, is unverified from the listing alone. We assess this as an unverified threat-actor claim involving alleged Brazilian municipal government and citizen data, NOT confirmation of a compromise of Cássia-MG systems. 🟠 위협 점수: 8/10 (높음)

### 1. 현재 주요 사이버보안 트렌드
최근 사이버 위협은 생성형 AI를 활용한 공격 자동화와 LLM 기반 시스템의 취약점을 노리는 방향으로 급격히 진화하고 있습니다. 특히 Claude Opus 5와 같은 고성능 AI 모델이 공격자의 계정 탈취 및 코드 실행을 위한 체인형 취약점 공격에 악용되는 사례가 보고되었습니다 ([TheHackerNews](https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/claude-opus-5-helped-researchers-take.html)). 또한, 공급망 공격의 일환으로 npm 패키지의 런타임 동작을 조작하여 보안 방어 체계를 우회하는 기법이 활발하며 ([BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/malicious-npm-packages-evade-install-script-defenses-at-runtime/)), AI 에이전트와 브라우저 확장 프로그램을 결합한 BragJack과 같은 새로운 형태의 공격이 등장했습니다 ([BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/bragjack-attacks-hijack-ai-browser-agents-through-malicious-extensions/)).

### 2. 주요 위협 행위자 / 캠페인
- **WaterPlum**: 구직자를 가장하여 악성코드를 유포하고 암호화폐 및 데이터를 탈취하는 캠페인 수행 ([CyberScoop](https://cyberscoop.com/north-korea-waterplum-job-seeker-crypto-attacks/))
- **Scattered Spider**: Ahmed Elbadawy 등 핵심 멤버가 검거되었으며, 대규모 사이버 범죄 행각으로 기소됨 ([CyberScoop](https://cyberscoop.com/scattered-spider-member-guilty-ahmed-elbadawy/))
- **NightEagle**: GhostContainer 백도어를 활용하여 러시아 기업을 타겟으로 Active Directory 취약점을 악용 ([Securelist](https://securelist.com/tr/nighteagle-apt-ghostcontainer-and-tunneling/121323/))
- **Toy Ghouls**: HiveMQ MQTT 브로커 및 Matrix 프로토콜을 C2로 사용하는 새로운 백도어 캠페인 포착 ([Securelist](https://securelist.com/toy-ghouls-new-hivemq-and-element-backdoors/121270/))

### 3. 한국 관련 위협
- **랜섬웨어 유포**: 'UBP 에셋'이라는 사설 HTS 프로그램을 악용한 랜섬웨어 유포 사례 확인 ([AhnLab ASEC](https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/95464/))
- **의료기관 타겟**: RDP 드라이브 리다이렉션 기능을 악용한 Beast(GodDamn) 랜섬웨어 공격 발생 ([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5779))
- **피싱 공격**: Slack의 정상적인 초대 기능을 악용한 임원 사칭 피싱 메일이 국내 기업 대상으로 유포 중 ([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5780))

### 4. 주요 CVE / 취약점
- **CVE-2026-76460**: Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE), CVSS 10.0, 인증 우회 취약점 ([DarkReading](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/cisco-zero-day-api-endpoint-authentication-issues))
- **CVE-2026-76461**: Cisco Secure Email Gateway, CVSS 9.8, 원격 코드 실행(RCE) 취약점 ([iss_kk_official](https://twitter.com/iss_kk_official/status/2101811727314944102))
- **CVE-2026-81294**: WordPress Authorizer 플러그인, CVSS 9.8, 인증되지 않은 원격 코드 실행 ([ridvanyagli](https://twitter.com/ridvanyagli/status/2101495296551227611))
- **CVE-2026-85706**: GitLab CE/EE, 경로 탐색(Path Traversal) 취약점 ([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5778))

### 5. IOC 요약

    - CVE-2026-76460 ([DarkReading](https://www.darkreading.com/vulnerabilities-threats/cisco-zero-day-api-endpoint-authentication-issues))
    - CVE-2026-85706 ([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5778))

- **Cisco 장비 점검**: Cisco ISE 및 Secure Email Gateway의 최신 보안 패치를 즉시 적용하고, 외부 노출 API 엔드포인트에 대한 접근 제어를 강화하십시오.
- **GitLab 업데이트**: GitLab CE/EE 사용자는 경로 탐색 취약점(CVE-2026-85706) 패치를 즉시 수행하여 저장소 커밋 API를 통한 공격을 차단하십시오.
- **피싱 대응**: Slack 등 협업 도구의 외부 초대 기능을 모니터링하고, 임원 사칭 메일에 대한 임직원 보안 교육 및 메일 필터링 정책을 강화하십시오.
